![A stylised magnetic field looping around a broken magnet](images/banner.jpg)

If you have ever played with fridge magnets, you know the golden rule of
magnetism: every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Push two north poles
together and they resist you. Flip one around and they snap together. It is a
simple, familiar fact: magnetic poles always come in pairs.

That leads to a natural question. If I cut a bar magnet in half, do I get one
piece that is purely north and another that is purely south? In the workshop,
the answer is no. Nature never hands you an isolated pole. Instead, you get two
smaller magnets, each complete with its own north and south pole. Cut again,
and you get four. Keep slicing down to the atomic level, and you still end up
with a two-poled dipole, never a single pole.

![Magnetic Dipoles](images/magnetic-dipoles.jpg)

So imagine my surprise when I first heard about magnetic monopoles:
hypothetical particles carrying only a single magnetic pole. How could
something like that even exist?

Yet for nearly a century, some of the greatest minds in physics have been
hunting for this rebel particle—an elementary charge that is pure north or pure
south, completely without the other. If monopoles exist, they would not just be
a curiosity. They would force us to rethink one of the deepest asymmetries in
nature: why electric charges exist as isolated particles, while magnetic
charges seem bound in pairs.

## The Great Asymmetry: Electricity vs Magnetism

To understand why physicists care so much about magnetic monopoles, we have to
look at magnetism's twin sibling: electricity.

Electricity and magnetism are two sides of the same coin: electromagnetism.
Yet when you look at how their charges behave, there is a glaring asymmetry:

- **Electric charges exist as monopoles:** You can isolate a single positive
  charge, like a proton, or a single negative charge, like an electron.
- **Magnetic charges only appear as dipoles:** Every magnet ever observed in
  free space carries both a north and a south pole.

In classical physics, this rule is written into one of the foundation stones of
electromagnetism: [Gauss's law for magnetism][gauss-law], one of the four
famous equations of [James Clerk Maxwell][maxwell]'s electromagnetic theory:

$$\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0$$

In plain English, this equation states that magnetic field lines never begin or
end. Unlike electric field lines, which radiate outward from positive charges
and terminate on negative charges, magnetic field lines always form continuous,
closed loops.

## Visualising the Difference: Dipole vs Monopole Fields

Comparing the field geometry of a familiar bar magnet against a hypothetical
monopole makes this mathematical difference immediately clear.

### 1. The Normal Magnet (Magnetic Dipole)

Because a normal magnet has no isolated magnetic charge acting as a starting
point, its field lines emerge from the north pole, curve through space to the
south pole, and continue through the magnet itself to complete the loop. If you
draw an imaginary closed surface anywhere around—or even partially through—the
magnet, every field line that enters must also leave. The net magnetic flux,
$\Phi_B$, is always zero.

![Magnets form closed loops](images/magnetic-closed-loops.jpg)

### 2. The Hypothetical Magnetic Monopole

If a magnetic monopole existed, its magnetic field would look just like the
electric field of a single proton or electron. The field lines would radiate
straight out into space for a north monopole, or point straight inward from all
directions for a south monopole:

$$\mathbf{B} \propto \frac{q_m}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf{r}}$$

![Hypothetical Magnetic Monopoles](images/magnetic-monopoles.jpg)

If we ever discover these particles, Maxwell's equations would become
beautifully symmetrical. That lonely zero in $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0$
would be replaced by a magnetic charge density, $\rho_m$.

## Why Do Physicists Think They Exist?

If we have never seen a fundamental magnetic monopole, why do so many
physicists suspect nature makes them anyway? There are two powerful theoretical
reasons.

### 1. Paul Dirac's 1931 Breakthrough

In 1931, the quantum pioneer [Paul Dirac][dirac] asked a deceptively simple
question: what would happen to quantum mechanics if a magnetic monopole
existed?

The answer stunned the physics community.

Dirac proved mathematically that if even a single magnetic monopole existed
anywhere in the cosmos, it would force all electric charges in the universe to
come in discrete, quantised packets. In other words, electric charge could not
take arbitrary values; it would have to come in multiples of a fundamental
unit.

That is precisely what we observe. Every free electron has a charge of
$-1e$, and every proton has a charge of $+1e$ (built from confined quarks with
exact thirds of $e$). Nothing carries an arbitrary charge like $0.374e$.
Without monopoles, classical physics had no baseline explanation for why charge
is quantised. With a monopole, quantisation follows as a mathematical
certainty.

As Dirac famously remarked, he would be surprised if nature had made no use of
this mechanism.

### 2. Grand Unified Theories (GUTs)

Physicists later found an even stronger reason. In Grand Unified Theories,
which merge the strong, weak, and electromagnetic forces at the extreme
temperatures of the early universe, monopoles are not merely allowed—they are
required.

As the newborn universe cooled and underwent phase transitions, knots in the
fabric of the unified field—known as topological defects—should have frozen
into place as ultra-heavy magnetic monopoles. These GUT monopoles would weigh
roughly $10^{16}$ times the mass of a proton, or about the mass of a single
bacterium packed into a subatomic point.

Why, then, is the universe not teeming with them? This puzzle—the *Monopole
Problem*—helped inspire the theory of cosmic inflation, which proposes that an
early burst of exponential expansion diluted these primordial relics across
vast cosmic distances. And because GUT monopoles are so massive, they are far
too heavy to forge inside human-made accelerators like the Large Hadron
Collider.

## Have We Found One Yet?

To date, no fundamental magnetic monopole has ever been confirmed in free
space. Still, the experimental trail features one famous cliffhanger and a
remarkable breakthrough in solid-state physics.

### The Valentine's Day Monopole (1982)

On 14 February 1982, physicist Blas Cabrera at Stanford University checked a
superconducting loop detector he had built in his lab. When an ordinary
magnetic dipole passes through a superconducting ring, the current jumps up and
then drops back to zero. A monopole, however, leaves a permanent, quantised
step in current.

That afternoon, Cabrera's instrument recorded the exact permanent jump of eight
flux quanta that a single Dirac monopole would produce. The physics world went
wild.

Then it never happened again. Years of larger, more sensitive follow-up
detectors failed to replicate the signal. Today, the "Valentine's Day Monopole"
remains one of the great cold cases in experimental science.

### Simulated Monopoles in Spin Ice

While the hunt for cosmic monopoles continues, condensed-matter physicists have
created the next best thing inside exotic crystals known as spin ices.

Inside a spin ice cooled near absolute zero, the magnetic moments of atoms sit
on a tetrahedral lattice. When energy is injected and a chain of tiny atomic
magnets flips, the north pole at one end of the chain and the south pole at the
other can untether from each other and hop independently from atom to atom.

Within the crystal, these emergent quasiparticles move and interact according
to the same mathematical laws as fundamental magnetic monopoles. They are not
elementary particles in free space, but they give physicists a laboratory
playground to test monopole dynamics firsthand.

Meanwhile, the search for fundamental monopoles presses on across two fronts:
cosmic observatories like [IceCube][icecube] in Antarctica watch for ancient,
ultra-heavy GUT relics from the Big Bang, while collider experiments like
[MoEDAL][moedal] at CERN hunt for lighter, TeV-scale monopoles predicted by
newer extensions to the Standard Model.

## The Takeaway

Next time you stick a note to your fridge, take a moment to appreciate how
strange that little magnet really is. Every magnet you have ever touched is a
closed loop of force, hiding a symmetry that physicists have spent nearly a
century trying to unlock.

Somewhere out there, left over from the dawn of time, a solitary magnetic pole
might still be drifting through the cosmos, waiting to complete the laws of
physics.
